claims.text: A uniform single-phase microstructure stabilized by high configurational entropy is critical for simultaneously achieving low density, high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance in lightweight HEAs.
Phase segregation or excessive lattice distortion degrades one or more of the targeted properties.
Arc melting followed by high-temperature homogenization can produce a minimally segregated, single-phase lightweight HEA.
A controlled post-synthesis heat treatment can induce partial phase separation or enhanced lattice distortion in the alloy.
Segregated or secondary phases, including nanoscale precipitates or intermetallics, act as internal-stress and corrosion or oxidation initiation sites.
High configurational entropy suppresses the formation of deleterious phases in a single-phase solid solution.
Suppression of deleterious phases ensures a uniform distribution of alloying elements.
Microstructural uniformity minimizes local stress concentrations.
Microstructural uniformity provides continuous barriers against crack initiation, corrosive attack, and oxidation.
Induced microstructural inhomogeneity creates regions of high internal stress and chemical instability.
Regions of high internal stress and chemical instability undermine mechanical, corrosion, and oxidation performance.
The homogeneous baseline alloy will have higher tensile strength than the heat-treated alloy with induced inhomogeneity.
The homogeneous baseline alloy will have a lower corrosion current density in 3.5 wt% NaCl than the inhomogeneous variant.
The homogeneous baseline alloy will form a more stable and adherent oxide scale at 800°C than the inhomogeneous variant.
At temperatures above approximately 1000°C or after prolonged exposure, even an initially homogeneous structure may degrade and lose its performance advantage.
Oxidation-driven phase transformations are a possible cause of degradation during sufficiently severe high-temperature exposure.
The proposed homogeneity mechanism may cease to apply when the alloy composition intrinsically favors segregation regardless of processing.
If induced inhomogeneity produces statistically comparable or better mechanical, corrosion, and oxidation performance than the homogeneous baseline, the proposed mechanism is falsified.
